newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Tough monitors needed for Albania poll - OSCE.
newsitem.headline: Tough monitors needed for Albania poll - OSCE.

text.p: Only foreigners of "strong mental and physical disposition" are advised to join a European group monitoring elections in nine days in Albania, the head of the operation said on Thursday.

"We really don't know from day to day where it is safe. This is something we have to monitor almost from hour to hour," said Tony Welch, heading an Organisation for Security and Cooperation in Europe (OSCE) monitoring operation.
He was speaking a day after an incident in which foreign troops, here to safeguard aid supplies, fired their first fatal shot at an Albanian.
Greek troops with a multinational protection force shot and killed an Albanian man in the central town of Elbasan, saying they got into a fight after he tried to sell them drugs.
"If we are fired at, we respond to the fire. If we are fired at directly, we respond to fire directly. Full stop," Italian-led force spokesman Giovanni Bernardi told journalists.
In the southern town of Girokaster, the OSCE said Romanian troops rescued 11 shaken foreign election monitoring staff, trapped by armed gangs in a restaurant for about an hour.

"Everyone who has come here has come as a volunteer ... there is absolutely no pressure on them whatsoever to stay," Welch told Reuters in an interview. But he added that so far no observers had decided to leave.

An interim government set up in March is racing to snap elections in a bid to restore calm after ex-Communist Albania collapsed into looting and violence following the failure of fraudulent investment schemes earlier this year.

Observers' safety is difficult to secure amid communication and military problems posed by Albania's mountainous, tough terrain, Welch said; it is already clear that there would be "black spots" OSCE observers will not reach.

A total of around 7,000 Italian-led troops will form a protection force for around 450 observers in the country on polling day, with around 6,500 already in place: but Welch said this was not as many as it sounds.
"Although six and half thousand troops sounds a lot, they're not a lot when you look at it in terms of ... the structure of the country -- very difficult to move around, very mountainous," he said.
Poor radio signals -- especially after dark when counting is scheduled to begin -- may pose further risks or hamper observers' mobility, he added.
"Movement after dark here does tend to be dangerous, so we would much prefer that the count was complete before the hours of darkness," he said.

With Albania's multi-party election organisers already missing deadlines in the run-up to the poll, Welch said delays in producing candidate lists may make voting on June 29 impossible in some areas, simply for lack of ballot papers.
"This is one of our worries," he said. By midday on Thursday the OSCE had received 67 lists out of a total of 115 electoral zones, and had been promised the rest by Friday.
"There cannot be an election in the zones we have not received the details for," he said. If areas fail again to meet the deadline, "there will certainly be a partial delay" in the poll.
Predicting difficult elections in Albania, which "already perhaps do not come up to the standards that we would wish", Welch nonetheless said he hoped shortcomings could be fixed.

The aim was to have an election satisfactory "to the people of Albania", he added. "As long as the thing doesn't go completely out of line, a missed deadline on the way to the finishing post is perhaps not so important."
